cards.subject: The Per ipsum and the little elevation at a Sunday Mass, seen from the back of a long stone nave, straight down the central aisle. The whole congregation kneels in the wooden pews, seen from behind, row after row, filling the church, the women's heads covered. Far off at the high altar beyond the altar rail, small, the priest, in a white-and-gold Roman fiddleback chasuble with the maniple on his left arm, over an amice and a lace-trimmed alb, seen from behind, facing the altar, holds the white Host above the golden chalice and lifts the two together a little above the altar; two servers kneel on the altar step; six tall candles burn on the gradine beside the crucifix and the white-veiled tabernacle, and morning light falls from the east window onto the raised Host. cards.subject: The Pax at a Solemn High Mass, seen at eye level from the choir, close to the sanctuary. At the middle of the high altar, the priest, in a white-and-gold Roman fiddleback chasuble with the maniple on his left arm, over an amice and a lace-trimmed alb, having kissed the altar, turns and embraces the deacon in his white dalmatic, their heads side by side, the priest's LEFT CHEEK beside the deacon's LEFT CHEEK, faces turned past each other (a formal liturgical embrace, NOT a kiss on the face), hands on each other's shoulders, giving him the kiss of peace; the subdeacon in a white tunicle waits behind to receive it in turn. In the foreground, in the carved choir stalls, a row of clerics in cassock and surplice stand with joined hands and bow as the peace comes toward them. Beyond the altar rail, soft and far, the faithful kneel in the pews. The gradine with six tall lit candles, the crucifix and the white-veiled tabernacle rise behind the embrace. Warm daylight from the side windows. Gentle, reconciled, sober. Keep everything inside the pointed arch. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides, and the arched window ending ABOVE the bottom band.
cards.frame: the inner window is a POINTED GOTHIC ARCH with slender gold tracery at its tip, like a sanctuary seen through a church arch; no halo

The handshake with a bow is the usual form in the US and in Brazil; the people stand (GIRM 43).

cards.subject: Holy Communion at a Sunday Mass, seen from the side at the altar rail, at eye level, looking along the line of communicants. Along the carved altar rail, draped with its white Communion cloth, the faithful kneel side by side with hands joined under the cloth. The priest, in a white-and-gold Roman fiddleback chasuble with the maniple on his left arm, over an amice and a lace-trimmed alb, stands in profile inside the rail holding a golden ciborium in his left hand, and with his right makes the sign of the cross with a white host over the ciborium before placing it on the tongue of an elderly woman in a black lace veil who kneels with head lifted and eyes lowered; beside him a server in cassock and surplice holds a golden Communion plate beneath her chin. Behind her, along the rail, a young man bows his head as he waits, and more of the faithful come up the aisle to kneel, small, hands joined: a girl in a white veil, a farmer, a mother with a baby on her hip. Beyond, the high altar with its lit candles on the gradine and the tabernacle open behind its white veil. Soft light, recollected joy. Keep everything inside the pointed arch. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides, and the arched window ending ABOVE the bottom band.
cards.frame: the inner window is a POINTED GOTHIC ARCH with slender gold tracery at its tip, like a sanctuary seen through a church arch; no halo

In the US, Communion is received standing, the communicant bowing the head before the Sacrament, on the tongue or in the hand (GIRM 160); the Communion-plate is prepared 'for the Communion of the faithful' (GIRM 118c). Communion under the one kind, so no chalice ministers.

cards.subject: The altar, as an illuminated still life: a traditional high altar of pale carved stone, seen from the front and slightly above the altar steps, which rise in three stone steps to a broad wooden foot-pace. The altar table is covered with three white linen cloths, the uppermost falling to the floor at either end; its front is hung with a white silk frontal embroidered in gold. Behind the table rise two stepped gradines, their tall candlesticks, crucifix and veiled tabernacle left in soft shadow at the top edge so that the table itself holds the eye; nothing stands on the table but its linen. On the gradine, low vases of white lilies and green leaves. Soft warm light on the stone, the gold and the linen. Dignified, bare, holy. No figures. The card's frame is exactly the attached cards': the coloured initial box at the top-left, one vine-and-flower band to its right along the top and one along the bottom, plain parchment margins down the sides; the deep-blue starred ground and its medallion sit between the two bands and end ABOVE the bottom band.
cards.frame: instead of the arched window, a centred gold-edged QUATREFOIL medallion on a deep blue ground scattered with small gold stars, holding a single object like an illuminated still life; no halo, no figures
cards.basis: The altar is 'the table of the Lord' (GIRM 296). It is built free-standing (GIRM 299). The table of a fixed altar is traditionally of natural stone (GIRM 301; wood is allowed in the US), and it carries 'at least one cloth, white in color' (GIRM 304). Flowers go 'around the altar rather than on the altar table' (GIRM 305). Only what the Mass needs is placed on the altar (GIRM 306), so outside Mass it is bare but for its cloth. The crucifix and candles are left to their own card, 'Altar crucifix and candles'.

sources.title: GIRM ch. 5, nos. 296–306 (the altar: table of the Lord, free-standing, natural stone, the white cloth, flowers around it)
GIRM ch. 4, nos. 117 (at least one white cloth)
